Header:
Date: 2026-02-10
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Li (Redwood SE), Jordan Park (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (CTO - Aurelius), Daniel Kim (Lead Infra - Aurelius), Marta Lopez (Security Architect - Aurelius), Alan Wu (ML Infra - Aurelius), Ruth Brennan (PM - Aurelius)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect): Deep dive re: private VPC deployment, networking, and runtime performance tradeoffs with focus on PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, DNS, KV cache and batching. Action items listed.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone thanks for joining, we have about an hour, appreciate you folks making time. quick intros?
[00:12] Priya: hi Priya here, CTO at Aurelius, i'm leading the infra side for this.
[00:18] Daniel: Daniel, lead infra engineer, i'll be doing the network setup.
[00:22] Marta: Marta, security architect.
[00:25] Alan: Alan, ML infra, i'll run the benchmark.
[00:30] Sofia: great, from Redwood i'm Sofia, AE, and Ethan and Jordan from SE will take us through the deep dive, particularly runtime and network patterns.
[00:40] Ethan: quick agenda: network placement options (PrivateLink vs public egress), NAT considerations, DNS and split-horizon, then runtime: batching, KV cache, quantization, and finally bench plan.
[01:05] Daniel: to set context, we're regulated, all traffic should not go over public internet, prefer interface endpoints or private link. also trying to minimize cross-AZ costs.
[01:20] Jordan: totally, we see that often. Redwood Private supports a data plane deployed into customer VPC where the inference nodes live in private subnets and talk to the control plane over a PrivateLink endpoint; can also run fully air-gapped variants if needed.
[01:35] Marta: couple compliance q's: do you require any outbound internet to download model artifacts? how do you handle KMS for keys?
[01:45] Ethan: good q. short answer: model artifacts and runtime images can be pre-staged into your private S3 or object storage via a presigned transfer or provided as an AMI/container image. KMS: we integrate with your KMS/HSM — keys stay in your account, Redwood's control plane just holds metadata. we can share the KMS integration doc.
[02:10] Priya: ok that helps. for networking, we want to avoid NAT for every subnet because of egress cost but also need to consider outbound control plane connectivity for metrics/tracing. how does PrivateLink work here?
[02:26] Ethan: PrivateLink uses interface endpoints in your VPC that create ENIs for the Redwood control plane, so control-plane traffic goes over AWS backbone to Redwood without hitting the public internet. in that model, the data plane (inference nodes) still needs to reach model store or images — but you can pre-stage those or use VPC endpoints to S3. so you can have zero public egress if you prefer.
[02:50] Daniel: so no NAT required if we pre-stage images and use interface endpoints for S3 and PrivateLink for control plane? any caveats around DNS?
[03:00] Jordan: you need split-horizon/private DNS for the interface endpoints so hostnames resolve to the private ENIs. we'll provide a recommended Route53 setup or you can inject a private hosted zone. the main caveat: if you have strict DNS forwarding or on-prem resolvers, you need to allow the VPC DNS resolver to resolve the private endpoints.
[03:20] Marta: cross-AZ traffic — if inference nodes in AZ A call S3 in AZ B, we incur cross-AZ charges. what's your recommendation?
[03:30] Ethan: place model store and inference nodes in the same AZ regions for large model loads. Redwood's scheduler prefers AZ-local placement when you request pinned subnets. for HA we distribute across AZs but for heavy model loads we advise keeping hotspot model artifacts local or use EFS mount with regional replication patterns.
[04:00] Alan: moving to runtime, can you outline the main latency contributors? we care about p95 and p99 for customer-facing features.
[04:10] Jordan: sure — at a high level: cold start / model load, token generation runtime (compute), network serialization/deserialization, and queueing from batching. KV cache hits are often the biggest win for repeated prefixes — a high cache hit rate can drop p95 by 30-60% depending on prompt distributions.
[04:40] Priya: what's the typical KV cache hit ratio you see?
[04:45] Ethan: it depends on workload; for chat-heavy workflows with system prompts and repeated instructions we often see 40-70% effective prefix reuse. for many few-shot prompts it's lower. we recommend running a sampling job of real traffic to estimate — we'll provide a small script.
[05:05] Daniel: batching — how does Redwood decide batch size vs latency? we need sub-second responses for some flows.
[05:12] Jordan: Redwood runtime uses dynamic batching tuned by a latency SLO. you set desired p95 latency and max batch size; the server waits up to a configurable microbatch timeout (e.g., 5-20ms) to aggregate. for sub-second SLOs we recommend smaller max batches (4-8) and aggressive microbatch timeouts. for throughput-oriented jobs (async embeddings) you can bump it up to 32-64.
[05:45] Marta: quantization — are you using 8-bit or lower? how does that affect accuracy and latency?
[05:50] Ethan: we support 8-bit and experimental 4-bit quantization profiles. 8-bit (GPTQ-style or AQT) gives 1.5-2x throughput improvements with minimal quality drop on many models; 4-bit can be 2-3x but with larger quality variance. for regulated customers we run evals on your prompt set to measure regression, and also provide model variants so you can choose accuracy vs cost.
[06:25] Alan: any differences in runtime when deployed in customer VPC vs Redwood hosted?
[06:30] Jordan: functionally none — the same binary/runtime. differences are in network topology (you control subnets and AZs), and some telemetry flows change: logs/metrics can be forwarded to your CloudWatch/Datadog via private endpoints. we instrument network egress and cross-AZ actually in our console so you can see cost drivers.
[07:00] Priya: about encryption — TLS between nodes is required? and do you terminate on the nodes?
[07:06] Ethan: yes TLS in transit between control plane and data plane and between management plane and nodes. for storage we support SSE-KMS and client-side encryption if you need.
[07:20] Ruth: on the topic of benchmarks — what's the recommended test harness for p95/p99?
[07:26] Jordan: we use a JMeter/Locust profile with realistic token lengths and concurrency, synthetic user think times. run with a warmup phase to populate KV cache and measure p50/p95/p99 after steady state. we'll share our load spec and a terraform module that spins up the test runners in your account to avoid egress.
[07:50] Daniel: curious about private link pricing and throughput. the ENIs have limits per AZ; any guidance on ENI scaling?
[07:57] Ethan: PrivateLink scales by adding more interface endpoints across subnets/AZs. for high control-plane throughput we recommend placing endpoints in each subnet group and using route tables to distribute. the control plane traffic is usually small (control messages, heartbeats), the data plane is heavy only for artifact transfers which you pre-stage.
[08:20] Priya: anything special for DNS when we have on-prem resolvers forwarding to Route53?
[08:25] Jordan: ensure the VPC resolver (169.254.169.253 or VPC provided) can resolve the interface endpoint's private zone; if you have conditional forwarders, create a private hosted zone and associate it with the VPC. if DNS is blocked/filtered, you can opt for IP-based endpoints but that's brittle — we prefer the private DNS solution.
[08:50] Alan: runtime perf numbers — can you share ballpark latency for typical LLM outputs? e.g., 512 tokens with context?
[08:58] Ethan: ballpark: for a 13B model on T4-like hardware (dense FP16), generation time per token ~25-40ms depending on attention implementation and KV cache. with 8-bit quant and optimized kernels on A100/NVIDIA H100 it's ~10-20ms per token. these are rough; key thing is KV cache — repeated prefixes can avoid recomputing earlier layers and drop end-to-end latency significantly.
[09:35] Priya: and for throughput — what's the QPS when batching?
[09:40] Jordan: it depends on batch size and sequence length. example: with batch size 16 on a 13B model you might get ~30-60 tokens/sec aggregate depending on hardware. embeddings and smaller models are obviously higher QPS.
[09:55] Daniel: for our flows we have mix: interactive chat (sub-second desired) and bulk generation (background). should we run mixed-mode benchmarks?
[10:03] Jordan: yes run mixed-profile: a low-latency lane with small batch + aggressive SLOs and a throughput lane that uses larger batches. Redwood supports multi-queue routing so you can route classes of traffic to different pools.
[10:25] Marta: audit logs — are they stored in our account or yours? retention options?
[10:30] Ethan: for Private deployments, logs/metrics can be forwarded to your sinks (CloudWatch, Splunk, Datadog) and kept under your retention policies. the Redwood control plane keeps metadata but can be configured to redact PII. we'll provide our retention and redaction guide.
[10:50] Alan: specific question on KV cache: how is cache coherence handled across multiple replicas?
[10:55] Jordan: KV cache is local to the GPU process for performance; for multi-replica scenarios we do warmup techniques and shared cache priming. we also support a shared redis-based prefix cache for non-latency-critical workloads but for lowest latency we rely on local KV cache and priming during deployment. note: local cache means slightly higher memory per replica but much lower latency.
[11:25] Priya: can you walk through a sample network layout — subnets, endpoints, security groups?
[11:30] Sofia: sure i'll share a diagram but quick verbal: you create private subnets in 3 AZs for inference nodes, an interface endpoint (PrivateLink) for control plane per AZ, gateway endpoint to S3 in each AZ for artifact access, route tables that do not route to an IGW for those subnets. security groups: allow control-plane port (we'll provide ports) from PrivateLink ENIs, allow inter-node traffic on gRPC ports, and limit egress to S3 endpoints.
[12:05] Daniel: do you require a bastion or do you have an operator plane?
[12:10] Jordan: we recommend a bastion/jump host for debugging but operationally we provide agent-based debug hooks that run via control plane over PrivateLink; you control whether to enable them.
[12:22] Marta: about NAT — you mentioned cost. can you quantify typical monthly NAT egress for a 5TB transfer?
[12:30] Ethan: NAT cost varies; egress to internet is the main expense. if you avoid internet egress (use S3 endpoints and PrivateLink) you'll avoid NAT traffic. 5TB egress to internet in us-east-1 could be thousands monthly; recommend pre-staging assets to avoid that.
[12:55] Alan: for benchmark we want to test cold starts vs warm. what's recommended?
[13:00] Jordan: run cold start tests by spinning nodes without preloaded model and measure model load time; then warm tests after a sustained load to populate KV caches and priming. for cold start minimization we have strategies: keep warm pools, deploy model shards pinned to instances, and pre-warm KV caches using recent prompts.
[13:25] Daniel: one more net question — how do you handle service discovery for the runtime pods inside our VPC?
[13:30] Ethan: the runtime registers with control plane via the PrivateLink ENI, and we provide an operator process that configures internal service discovery via tags and Route53 SRV records if you want internal name resolution. otherwise communication is via explicit IPs/security groups we supply in templates.
[14:00] Priya: ok let's talk telemetry and cost visibility — we want token-level cost breakdowns per route.
[14:06] Jordan: Redwood Console shows token-level cost and latency per model and route. for Private we can push the same metrics into your Datadog via private endpoint so you can correlate with infra cost.
[14:25] Alan: performance regression detection — we want alerts on model quality slips after quantization.
[14:30] Ethan: Redwood Optimize runs evals against your golden prompts and raises regression alerts. for private deployments we can run those evals in your account or accept masked sample data. we'll set up a webhook for alerts.
[14:50] Ruth: any known gotchas with cross-account IAM roles for S3?
[14:55] Jordan: ensure roles are scoped to the exact bucket prefixes where artifacts live and avoid wildcard principals. we provide a minimal IAM policy for the runtime to read model artifacts, and recommend using an artifact bucket per environment.
[15:15] Daniel: operational question — how do upgrades happen for runtime?
[15:20] Ethan: rolling upgrades are controlled by you; the control plane can orchestrate canary deploys and fallbacks. for Private deployments you can opt-in to automatic upgrades or pull updates manually. we support version pinning per deployment.
[15:40] Priya: good. can we get a sample terraform module to provision endpoints and security groups?
[15:45] Sofia: yes we'll share that — action item.
[15:50] Jordan: going back to runtime knobs: microbatch timeout, max batch size, and concurrency per GPU are the three levers you can tune. smaller microbatch timeout lowers latency at cost of throughput. increasing GPU concurrency improves throughput but can add latency jitter in high tail scenarios.
[16:15] Alan: for our chat UI we need avg latency < 700ms p95 for short dialogs. is that realistic in private VPC?
[16:21] Ethan: yes on smaller models or with high KV cache hit rates. combination: use smaller batch sizes for that route, pin dedicated low-latency pool (smaller instance types tuned for latency) and ensure AZ placement is local to your app servers. shared pools will have more variability.
[16:45] Marta: security follow-up: do you provide attestations for network config?
[16:50] Sofia: yes we'll provide configuration checklists and a network validation guide.
[17:00] Daniel: if we want to run the benchmark in our account, what access do you need?
[17:05] Jordan: minimal IAM to create test runners and S3 buckets for logs; we'll provide a least-privilege terraform module. also we'll need the CIDR ranges and preferred subnets so we can propose endpoint placements.
[17:25] Priya: let's define SLOs: p95 <= 700ms for chat route, p99 < 2s for critical flows, background throughput for batch jobs measured by tokens/sec.
[17:40] Ethan: noted. we'll draft a bench plan with those targets.
[18:00] Alan: short question: do you support multi-tenant isolation within a single VPC?
[18:05] Jordan: yes via namespace isolation and security groups; for strict isolation you can set up dedicated clusters per team or use separate subnets and RBAC controls.
[18:20] Daniel: what about metrics cardinality — will pushing all token-level traces blow up our monitoring costs?
[18:26] Ethan: we recommend sampling token-level traces and aggregating metrics; we send high-level traces to your sinks, and for detailed debug you can enable full traces per-request on a small sample.
[18:45] Marta: any timeline constraints you recommend for POC?
[18:50] Sofia: typical POC is 4-6 weeks: week 1 network + terraform provisioning, week 2 model staging and runtime config, week 3 benchmark and iteration, week 4 wrap-up and cost/accuracy tradeoff review.
[19:10] Daniel: sounds good. we'll pencil 4 weeks.
[19:15] Jordan: quick perf note: we recommend starting with 8-bit quant and run regressions; many customers see ~1.8x improvement with minimal quality loss.
[19:35] Alan: do you provide sample prompt eval suite to test quality regression post-quant?
[19:40] Ethan: yes we'll share the eval harness and example prompts; you can run locally or in your account.
[19:55] Priya: question on cross-region replication — if we want DR in another region, do you replicate models or pull at startup?
[20:02] Jordan: we recommend replicating model artifacts to the DR region to avoid long cold-starts; we can automate replication or provide scripts you run.
[20:20] Marta: any expected differences for on-prem (air-gapped) vs VPC private cloud?
[20:25] Ethan: on-prem requires packaging runtime images and model artifacts into your air-gapped registry and manual installation. latency characteristics are similar but ops overhead is higher; we provide an ops runbook.
[20:45] Alan: let's capture the benchmark plan specifics — what samples and what metrics?
[20:50] Jordan: plan: 1) traffic sample (we'll share script), 2) warmup phase to prime KV cache, 3) latency lane (low batch size) measuring p50/p95/p99 and tail jitter, 4) throughput lane (large batches) measuring tokens/sec and cost per token, 5) quantization runs (FP16 vs 8-bit vs 4-bit) measuring quality regression and latency. metrics: p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, cross-AZ egress bytes.
[21:25] Daniel: okay. for the S3 endpoints you mentioned gateway endpoints are preferred to avoid NAT for artifact access?
[21:30] Ethan: yes gateway endpoints for S3 avoid NAT. for ECR you can use interface endpoints or VPC endpoints if needed.
[21:45] Priya: you mentioned a shared redis-based prefix cache as an option — what are the tradeoffs?
[21:50] Jordan: shared redis prefix cache gives global reuse across replicas but adds network hop latency; it's good for higher-latency tolerant workloads or to reduce cold-start load on GPUs. for lowest latency we prefer local KV cache.
[22:10] Alan: how do you measure KV cache hit rate in the console?
[22:15] Jordan: we emit metrics per shard: kv_cache.hits and kv_cache.misses and percentage. also per-route metrics so you can see which routes benefit most.
[22:30] Marta: okay this is great. curious about fallback policies — if a dedicated pool is saturated what's the failover path?
[22:36] Ethan: you can configure routing policies: failover to a compatible model variant in the same VPC, route to hosted Redwood pool (if allowed), or queue the request. for private-only deployments we recommend pre-allocated burst capacity or autoscaling policies.
[22:55] Daniel: autoscaling in a private VPC — do you need additional permissions for creating new ENIs or subnets?
[23:00] Jordan: autoscaling will create/terminate instances in the subnets you register; ensure instance profile allows EC2 actions and ENI creation. we'll include the minimal IAM.
[23:20] Priya: any tips for reducing cross-AZ latencies?
[23:25] Ethan: co-locate app servers and inference nodes in same AZ, use local S3 caches where possible, and pin models to AZ-local pools for latency-critical routes.
[23:40] Sofia: wrapping toward next steps — we'll share terraform modules, security pack, eval harness, and bench plan. Ethan will own the benchmarking run.
[23:54] Daniel: i'll gather the CIDR/subnet info and share this afternoon.
[24:00] Marta: expect security questions on key rotation and audit logging — i'll put those in writing.
[24:08] Ruth: schedule the follow-up review in two weeks to look at preliminary bench results?
[24:12] Sofia: sounds good, we'll target 2026-02-24 for a bench review — i'll send calendar invite.
[24:22] Jordan: final quick note on network egress cost: avoid NAT and use S3 + PrivateLink to keep egress on AWS backbone; for cross-region replication budget accordingly.
[24:40] Alan: thanks all.
[24:42] Priya: thanks, very helpful.
[24:45] Sofia: thanks we'll send the artifacts.
[24:48] END OF TRANSCRIPT (remaining minutes used for follow-up q&a and informal discussion)
